name: Cold showers

lead: Cold showers are taken for claimed benefits to skin, hair, testosterone, mood and discipline. Users post that skin and hair look better; others say cold showers make eye bags or features look harsher.

Cold exposure triggers the cold shock response, vasoconstriction and a surge in the sympathetic nervous system, and repeated cold showers reduce the initial response to later cold immersion. Meta-analyses of cold-water exposure report pooled signals toward better mood, perceived stress and wellbeing, with wide confidence intervals. No study has tested cold showers for skin appearance or testosterone.

paras: People end a normal shower with a cold blast or take the whole shower cold, often as a morning routine, building up duration over days to weeks. It overlaps with ice baths, cold plunges and the Wim Hof Method.

Cold-water immersion can cause gasping, heart rate and blood pressure surges, and arrhythmias in some people. The American Heart Association and British Heart Foundation advise consulting a physician before cold therapy. Combining breath-holding or hyperventilation with water has been linked to blackout and drowning reports.

web.title: The Effect of Cold Showering on Health and Work: A Randomized Controlled Trial

angle.text: Users take cold showers expecting tighter-looking, healthier skin, better hair and a mood and discipline lift, through a circulation and stress-response jolt. Meta-analyses report mood and stress effects; skin, hair and hormone claims come from user reports.

lead: Cold showers are showers taken with cold water, either for the whole wash or as a cold finish after warm water. In looksmaxxing and self-improvement communities they are used for claimed effects on skin, hair, testosterone, mood and discipline, and some users describe them as a daily habit that supports a leaner, more consistent routine.[1][2] The practice sits in the same family as ice baths, cold plunges, winter swimming and the Wim Hof Method.[3][4]

Looks-related claims are the part most specific to this community. Posters say cold water leaves skin and hair in better shape, reduces shedding and tightens the look of the face, while others argue the opposite, that cold exposure makes features appear harsher or worsens under-eye bags.[5][6][7] Neither side cites appearance trials, because none have been published.

Research on cold-water exposure is broader. A 2025 PLOS ONE systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials in healthy adults listed skin health among its outcomes, and a 2026 meta-analysis of 13 studies found pooled estimates generally favoured cold-water exposure for depressive symptoms, perceived stress, wellbeing and mood, with wide confidence intervals and smaller effects when only controlled studies were counted.[8][9] A large Dutch randomized trial of ending showers with cold water reported fewer sick days taken from work.[10] Popular interest has been lifted by figures such as Wim Hof and by podcasters who have promoted ice baths.[3][4]
infobox: Water at or below 15 degrees Celsius for at least 30 seconds [8]

paras: Cold showers use water below a comfortable temperature, from brief cold finishes at the end of a warm shower to fully cold showers. Studies of cold-water immersion define the exposure as water at or below 15 degrees Celsius for at least 30 seconds, delivered through showers, ice baths or plunges.[8] In the Dutch Cool Challenge trial, intervention groups ended their usual hot shower with 30, 60 or 90 seconds at the coldest setting available.[10]

Cold-water exposure produces what physiologists call the cold shock response: skin cooling causes blood vessels near the surface to constrict, breathing becomes rapid, the gasp reflex appears and heart rate rises. The initial phase typically lasts a few minutes and is strongest when the skin cools quickly.[11] Regular exposure appears to blunt this initial response through habituation.[12][11]

Cold showers also have a long place in physiology research. A 1964 Journal of Applied Physiology paper studied cardiovascular responses to ice-cold showers, and a 1970 study examined how the length of a cold shower affects skin temperature and exercise heart rate.[13][14] A 2001 randomized trial in 16 marathon runners tested a whole-body cold shower before a race and reported a difference in the CK-MB/CK ratio but no difference in muscle soreness or CK.[15]

sections.h: How people use cold showers for their looks
paras: In looksmaxxing forums the practice is usually described in general terms: finishing a shower cold, switching to cold water for hair washing, or committing to cold showers as a daily discipline. Users pair it with other routines, including no-poo hair care, nofap and sauna sessions.[5][16][17]

Skin and hair are the main appearance goals. Posters say cold water leaves skin looking better and hair in better condition, and one thread frames cold showers as an anti-hair-loss measure.[2][5][6] Another thread asks directly whether cold or hot showers are better for skin.[17] A recurring theme is leanmaxxing: one poster lists cold showers alongside effects on sperm count and gynecomastia in a thread other members treated as humorous.[1]

A second use is psychological. Several early looksmax.org threads, by their titles, describe cold showers as a 'cope destroyer' or something that 'destroys' fake copes, a framing in which the shower is a test of toughness.[18][19] A T Nation member similarly lists cold showers among uncomfortable habits that build courage and flexibility.[20]

Posters claim cold showers improve skin and hair, reduce hair loss, support testosterone and discipline, and act as a 'cope destroyer' that builds mental toughness.[5][18][6] Some say they help with premature ejaculation, sperm count and gynecomastia, claims made in a thread that other members treated as humorous.[1]

Sceptical members of the same forum hold differing views. One poster says cold showers give a harsher look, with denser beard and body hair and worse eye bags, attributing it to circulation and blood pressure; a reply objects to the 'cortisol spike' and vasoconstriction.[7] Other threads question whether the habit is overrated, with thread titles such as 'cant belive i used to torture myself with cold showers' and one that sets out to debunk cold showers and nofap as 'copes'.[21][16]

A separate stream of belief comes from the hormesis idea, that brief, intermittent stressors may produce adaptive benefits. Hormesis is a dose-response concept in which low doses of a stressor stimulate and high doses inhibit; its mechanisms are described as still under early laboratory research, and its wider claims are debated in toxicology.[22] A 2008 hypothesis paper applied a related idea to cold showers, proposing that adapted cold showers could be a treatment for depression.[23]

sections.h: Wim Hof Method and the cold-plunge scene
paras: The Wim Hof Method, developed by Dutch extreme athlete Wim Hof (born 20 April 1959), combines cold exposure, breathing techniques and meditation or willpower. Cold showers are a standard entry point for followers.[3] Hof gained attention for records, including a 2000 Guinness record for swimming under ice and a 2007 attempt on Everest in shorts, and he has published books and appeared in documentaries.[3]

A 2011 Radboud University study of the method was broadcast on Dutch television in April 2011, and a 2024 meta-analysis of eight studies found the method may reduce inflammation, possibly via increased epinephrine, with mixed findings on exercise and respiratory outcomes; its authors described the studies as very low quality, with small samples and mostly male participants.[3]

More broadly, ice baths and cold plunges have been popularized by endurance athletes such as marathon runner Paula Radcliffe and swimmer Michael Phelps, and by podcasters including Joe Rogan and Andrew Huberman, according to Wikipedia.[4] Cold showers are the lowest-barrier version of this trend and are commonly recommended in forums as a starting point, though the forums rarely draw the distinction between showers and the longer baths studied in most trials.[8][4]

The 2025 PLOS ONE meta-analysis included 11 randomized studies with 3,177 participants, almost all using baths rather than showers, at water temperatures from 7 to 15 degrees Celsius, and listed skin health among the outcomes it evaluated.[8] The 2026 Frontiers in Physiology meta-analysis of 13 studies with 4,105 participants found pooled estimates favoured cold exposure for depression symptoms, perceived stress, wellbeing and mood, little consistent benefit for anxiety, and sparse data on sleep, cortisol, heart rate and pain.[9]

A 2008 hypothesis paper proposed adapted cold showers as a potential treatment for depression, and a 2005 study in 18 people found that six repeated cold showers over four days reduced the initial responses to a later 3-minute immersion in 10 degree water.[23][12] Related hypothesis papers from the same period proposed repeated cold stress for chronic fatigue and hydrotherapy as a sedative.[24][25]

Two randomized trials of the Wim Hof Method, which combines fast-paced breathing with cold showers, in women with high stress and depressive symptoms compared it with slow-breathing controls; in one trial all four arms improved with no group differences at the end of the intervention.[26][27]

Wikipedia reports that a 2024 meta-analysis of the Wim Hof Method judged most studies to be of very low quality, and that the American Heart Association and British Heart Foundation advise consulting a physician before cold therapy.[3] On sport recovery, a 2012 Cochrane review is reported to have found some evidence that ice baths reduce post-exercise soreness, and a 2024 meta-analysis is reported to have found cold immersion right after resistance training may blunt muscle growth, with the authors noting the studies were of fair to poor quality.[4]

The largest trial of cold showering is the Cool Challenge, a pragmatic, unblinded randomized trial in the Netherlands published in PLOS ONE on 15 September 2016 by Geert Buijze and colleagues. It randomized 3,018 adults aged 18 to 65 who did not routinely shower cold into four groups: usual showers, or showers ended with 30, 60 or 90 seconds of the coldest water available, for 30 days, followed by a 60-day period in which participants chose their own routine.[10]

Cold showering was associated with a 29 percent reduction in self-reported sickness absence from work (incidence rate ratio 0.71), with no differences between the three durations, while the number of illness days did not differ significantly. The authors listed self-reporting, the lack of blinding and loss to follow-up as limitations.[10] The trial did not assess skin, hair or appearance.

Cold shock can cause gasping, hyperventilation, a faster heart rate and a sharp rise in cardiac workload, and can contribute to arrhythmias, especially in people with heart disease; breath-holding time falls sharply in water below about 15 degrees Celsius.[11] Wikipedia reports that cold-water immersion can trigger heart arrhythmias in healthy people.[3]

The Wim Hof breathing exercises can cause hyperventilation and potentially fatal blackout if done in water, and Wikipedia reports 32 alleged deaths linked to the method as of March 2024, including drownings in 2015 and 2016, a 2021 pool drowning in Singapore and a 2022 death in the UK; a 2022 lawsuit over a teenager's drowning in California was dismissed in July 2024.[3] Journalist Scott Carney released a 2023 documentary linking 13 deaths to the method.[3]

Medical bodies are cited as advising caution with cold therapy generally, and ice baths are described as carrying risks including hypothermia and cardiac stress.[3][4] For people interested in appearance specifically, the forum concern that cold exposure worsens eye bags or facial look is untested.[7]

No studies found of cold showers for skin appearance, hair or testosterone. Human research examines mood, stress and wellbeing outcomes of cold-water exposure, habituation to cold, sickness absence after cold showering, muscle soreness around exercise, and the Wim Hof Method for depressive symptoms.[8][9][12][26][10][15]

Cold showers are a recurring topic on looksmax.org, discussed as a skin and hair aid, a discipline tool, a source of jokes, and, by some, a downside for appearance.[2][5][7] Posts about them are often tied to nofap, sauna and no-poo routines and to the 'cope' vocabulary used across the forum.[18][16][17] Outside the looks forums the habit appears in strength-training communities such as T Nation, where members mention taking cold showers in winter, using them for discipline, or trying a Wim Hof style routine for immunity.[28][20][29]

Hacker News discussion of the idea that cold showers and exercise share a hormetic logic reached 198 points and 135 comments in 2016, showing the practice's spread into general self-improvement circles.[30]
